claims.text: Preheating the build substrate to approximately 500–600 °C during additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi will slow the cooling rate.
Substrate preheating will reduce compositional segregation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Substrate preheating will minimize residual thermal stresses in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Substrate preheating will lower defect formation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Reduced segregation, residual stress, and defect formation will improve the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi relative to processing without substrate preheating.
Preheating will produce a more compositionally homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure.
Preheating the substrate reduces thermal gradients during solidification.
Reduced thermal gradients moderate the rapid cooling rate.
Moderating the cooling rate limits segregation of the constituent elements.
Reduced thermal gradients and moderated cooling suppress residual-stress development.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi samples will have greater toughness than non-preheated additively manufactured controls.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi samples will have greater yield strength than non-preheated additively manufactured controls.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi samples will have a lower density of internal defects than non-preheated additively manufactured controls.
The proposed effects are valid for powder-bed-fusion processing in an inert atmosphere with substrate temperatures around 500–600 °C.
Processing outside the stated temperature range or with other processing techniques may produce different outcomes.
Similar observations in related alloys support the proposed mechanism.
Substrate preheating may cause microstructural coarsening that offsets some benefits of reduced thermal stress.
